\title{\textbf{Predicting vortex shedding behind a circular cylinder\\
with physics-informed neural networks}}

\begin{abstract}
\noindent
A data-free physics-informed neural network (PINN) applied to the unsteady
wake of a circular cylinder is known to lose the wake and fall towards the
steady symmetric solution, which satisfies the governing equations exactly.
This project reproduces that failure on purpose-generated lattice Boltzmann
ground truth, validated at $\Rey = 100$ against Qu et al.\ ($\St$ within
$0.04\%$, $\Cd$ $3.5\%$ high), and measures what defeats it. Two confounds had
inflated the project's own earlier results, and both are now controlled. One is
how many slices of ground truth a run sees; the other is the phase of the
shedding cycle at which it starts. With one slice and four start phases averaged over five seeds, a plain
PINN keeps 31.1\% of the reference wake amplitude. Causal time-marching raises
that to 56.4\%, although at equal training budget it adds only 7.7 points, less
than the 17.5 that training longer adds on its own. Only with Fourier features
and a Reynolds decomposition as well does the result stop depending on the
start phase: 72.9\% retained, at a velocity-field error of 0.031. Over five
chained periods that configuration sheds 10.4\% slow and ends about half a
cycle out of phase. Re-anchoring it with 350 supervised points per shedding
period, about 2\% of the reference data that per-window snapshots use, holds
the phase over all five. A few hundred supervised points per window close most of the remaining
gap in amplitude.
Across $\Rey = 60$--$180$ the three mechanisms keep 63--79\% of the wake
against 24--45\% for the plain network. A recurrent sequence PINN is no
substitute for marching: it keeps less of the wake than the plain network,
marched or not. Adding the governing equations to a neural-operator forecast
does not help on the validated data. On an earlier, harder dataset it extends
a Fourier Neural Operator's useful horizon, but it is neutral for a U-Net and
harmful for a convolutional GRU, so the benefit depends on the backbone.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction and objective}

Above $\Rey \approx 47$ the wake behind a circular cylinder becomes unstable
and sheds a K\'arm\'an vortex street at a frequency characterised by the
Strouhal number $\St = fD/U$. Predicting that shedding with a neural network
is hard for three structural reasons:

\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{The steady solution remains a valid solution.} A symmetric,
        non-shedding field satisfies the Navier--Stokes equations and every
        boundary condition exactly. It is unstable physically, but a PINN loss
        measures residuals, not stability, so the steady field is an easily
        reachable minimum.
  \item \textbf{Spectral bias.} Networks fit low-frequency content long before
        high-frequency content, which directly opposes representing an
        oscillatory wake.
  \item \textbf{The initial condition is a measure-zero slice} of the
        space--time domain, and is therefore weakly weighted against the bulk
        PDE residual that fills it.
\end{enumerate}

The documented consequence\,\cite{chuang2023} is that a data-free PINN
``behaves like a steady solver'', while a data-driven one sheds only where
data is present. Two points of scope. First, their cylinder case is at
$\Rey = 200$, solved as a \emph{single} time window spanning forty shedding
periods. This project reproduces the phenomenon at $\Rey = 100$, and across
$\Rey = 60$--$180$ in Section~\ref{sec:resweep}, from a baseline that solves
one window of one period. That is a much easier setting than theirs, and the
baseline still loses most of the wake. Second, they attribute the collapse to
spectral bias, on the evidence of a Koopman analysis showing damped modes. The
ablation below finds that attacking spectral bias directly does not, on its
own, keep more of the wake. Enforcing causality does, and does most in
combination with the other two mechanisms.

The objective is to reproduce that failure on validated ground truth
of our own, and then to establish \emph{which} mechanism defeats it, with an
ablation controlled well enough that the answer is attributable. The
mechanism that works, causal time-marching, is not new in itself: it is the
sequence-to-sequence formulation of Krishnapriyan et
al.\,\cite{krishnapriyan2021}, demonstrated there on one-dimensional
convection, reaction and reaction--diffusion problems, and a hard-window
relative of the causal weighting of Wang et al.\,\cite{wang2024causality}.
What is measured here is how much it contributes on two-dimensional wake
shedding without data, separated from the extra training a marched run
receives, and how it interacts with the other two mechanisms. Chuang and
Barba\,\cite{chuang2023} report that some form of data supervision is
necessary to sustain shedding at all. So does Shah\,\cite{shah2026}, more
recently, who ablates six techniques on a confined cylinder benchmark and finds
that only supervised combinations escape the collapse. Neither tests hard
time-window marching. The answer found here sits between: a data-free marched
chain does sustain a wake, at three-quarters of its amplitude, but only with
all three mechanisms together, and over five periods it drifts about half a
cycle out of phase with the reference. Holding the phase does take data, but
little: 350 supervised points per shedding period.

A second thread connects the work to its reference paper. Renn et
al.\,\cite{renn2023} forecast subcritical cylinder wakes with a Fourier Neural
Operator (FNO) that is \emph{purely data-driven}; there is no physics term
anywhere in it. Section~\ref{sec:fno} tests whether adding physics to such an
operator improves forecast stability, for the FNO and for two other common
forecasting backbones. Section~\ref{sec:arch} asks the corresponding question of the PINN:
whether a sequence architecture proposed against PINN failure modes does the
job of marching.

\paragraph{Reynolds number.} The ablation and the accuracy study are at
$\Rey = 100$: laminar and two-dimensional. Renn et al.'s
$\Rey = 240$--$3060$ is three-dimensional, where a 2-D model would be
solving the wrong physics. Section~\ref{sec:resweep} repeats the central
comparison across $\Rey = 60$--$180$, the upper limit set by the
three-dimensional transition at $\Rey_c = 188.5 \pm 1.0$\,\cite{barkley1996}.

\paragraph{Software.} The work builds on \texttt{underPINN}, a JAX PINN
framework, which supplies the MLP and Fourier-feature networks, the FNO, the
geometry primitives and a steady Navier--Stokes residual. The unsteady operator
(Section~\ref{sec:operator}), the lattice Boltzmann solver, the ablation
machinery, the operator-forecasting code and the sequence, U-Net and ConvGRU
networks of Sections~\ref{sec:arch} and~\ref{sec:fno} are contributions of
this project.

\section{Ground truth by lattice Boltzmann}
\label{sec:lbm}

No experimental data was available, so the reference wake is generated. The
solver (\texttt{src/cfd/\allowbreak lbm\_cylinder.py}) is a D2Q9 two-relaxation-time (TRT)
lattice Boltzmann method written in JAX.

\paragraph{Solver choices.}
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{TRT collision.} A single-relaxation-time (BGK) scheme places
        the bounce-back wall at a viscosity-dependent position, so the
        cylinder's effective diameter drifts with $\Rey$. TRT relaxes the
        symmetric and antisymmetric parts separately, allowing the magic
        parameter $\Lambda = (\tau^+ - 1/2)(\tau^- - 1/2)$ to be pinned at
        $3/16$, which fixes the wall location.
  \item \textbf{Half-way bounce-back} for the no-slip cylinder, placing the
        wall midway between nodes, and \textbf{momentum exchange} for the
        surface force.
  \item \textbf{Specular (free-slip) top and bottom walls}, enforcing $v = 0$
        exactly and matching the symmetry condition used on the PINN side.
  \item \textbf{An absorbing layer} of $8D$ at each free-slip wall, relaxing
        the populations toward the free-stream equilibrium at a peak rate of
        $0.05$ per step on a cubic ramp, with $\tau^-$ recomputed pointwise so
        that $\Lambda$ stays exactly $3/16$. Section~\ref{sec:acoustic}
        explains why it is needed.
  \item \textbf{The inlet $25D$ ahead of the cylinder}, in a domain $60D$ long.
\end{itemize}

Shedding is triggered by a brief transverse inlet perturbation; without it the
symmetric base flow persists indefinitely (the same degeneracy that the PINN
later falls into, appearing here in the reference solver).

\paragraph{Production dataset.} $\Rey = 100$, $D = 24$ lattice units,
$\mathrm{Ma} = 0.087$, grid $1440 \times 1200$, blockage $D/H = 2\%$. The saved
record is 641 snapshots covering 20 shedding periods, on a $241 \times 121$
grid at $\Delta x = 0.083D$ and $\Delta \tstar = 0.19$, chosen near the
reference paper's PIV resolution so that the later comparison is like-for-like.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{Validation of the ground truth at $\Rey = 100$. Benchmarks are Qu et
al.\,\cite{qu2013}: the range is their compilation of eight independent
large-domain studies, and the errors are taken against their own values,
$\Cd = 1.317$, $\St = 0.1649$ and $\Cl' = 0.2224$.}
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
quantity & computed & benchmark\,\cite{qu2013} & error \\
\midrule
$\Cd$ (mean drag coefficient)  & 1.3634 & 1.318--1.336 & $+3.5\%$ \\
$\St$ (Strouhal number)        & 0.1648 & 0.164--0.166 & $-0.04\%$ \\
$\Cl'$ (r.m.s.\ lift)          & 0.2362 & 0.222--0.235 & $+6.2\%$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\label{tab:validation}
\end{table}

$\St$ is measured from wake vorticity, which cannot see irrotational sound; the
lift and a single wake probe give the same value to within $0.002\%$. The
remaining $\Cd$ offset is resolution, quantified below: at $D = 32$ the same
geometry gives $+2.3\%$.

\subsection{How the ground truth was validated}
\label{sec:acoustic}

An earlier version of this dataset put the inlet $8D$ ahead of the cylinder and
had no absorbing layer. It read $\St = 0.1595$ ($-3.3\%$) and $\Cd = 1.3798$,
and was reported as agreeing with a benchmark of 1.37--1.38 to $0.3\%$; that
benchmark was uncited and closer to the $\Rey = 200$ value. Three problems
were found and fixed, each by a controlled test (Figure~\ref{fig:validation}).

\paragraph{The domain is a duct, and the duct resonates.} Free-slip walls
reflect sound perfectly and lattice Boltzmann carries real sound, so the domain
supports a transverse standing half-wave at $c_s/2H$ (in flow units
$\St_a = (c_s/2H)(D/U) = 0.1155$). Given time it captures the wake itself: with
no absorbing layer, wake vorticity sheds at $\St = 0.1600$ over 20 recorded
periods and at $0.1132$ over 38, on the resonance. A viscosity ramp, the
textbook absorbing layer, does nothing here (0.1131): viscous absorption scales
as $\nu\omega^2$ and this mode's wavelength is twice the domain height, so an
$8D$ layer at twenty times the viscosity removes about $0.04\%$ of the
amplitude per pass. Relaxing toward the free stream damps at a rate set per
step, independent of frequency, and releases the wake ($0.1694$ over the same
38 periods). The result does not depend on the layer: across a twofold change
in its width and a fivefold change in its rate, $\Cd$ moves by $0.1\%$ and
$\St$ by $0.2\%$, and 38 and 120 recorded periods agree to four figures.

Blevins\,\cite{blevins1985} showed experimentally that a transverse acoustic
wave shifts cylinder shedding to its own frequency through the acoustic
velocity rather than the pressure, and Hong et al.\,\cite{hong2020} model the
coupling for a cylinder in a duct, placing the lock-in band at
$\St/\St_a \le 1.14$. At $\Rey = 100$ the ratio here is $1.43$, well outside
that band, and the wake still locks given enough time, plausibly because
lossless walls sustain the mode at separations a physical duct could not. The
practical consequence was that no dataset could be recorded for long enough to
average force coefficients over the 80-odd cycles the literature uses.

\paragraph{Inlet distance and blockage.} With the absorbing layer in
place and the grid converged, crossing domain height ($H = 50D$, $120D$) with
inlet distance ($8D$, $25D$) separates the two geometric suspects.
Moving the inlet from $8D$ to $25D$ ahead of the cylinder lowers $\Cd$ by
$4.7\%$, from $+7.4\%$ to $+2.3\%$ against Qu et al., and takes $\St$ from
$+3.0\%$ to $+0.3\%$; raising the height from
$50D$ to $120D$ moves $\Cd$ by $0.36\%$, and by $0.07\%$ once the inlet is far
enough upstream. Posdziech and Grundmann, as reported by Qu et
al.\,\cite{qu2013}, require more than $20D$. Blockage was never the dominant
error.

\paragraph{Resolution.} At fixed geometry, $\Cd = 1.4334$, $1.4139$ and $1.4147$
at $D = 24$, $32$ and $48$: converged at $D = 32$, with $D = 24$ about $1.4\%$
high in $\Cd$ and within $0.3\%$ in $\St$. The production dataset keeps
$D = 24$ so that its snapshot grid matches the PIV-like resolution the networks
are trained on; the price is the $\Cd$ offset in Table~\ref{tab:validation}.

\paragraph{Residual divergence.} Lattice Boltzmann is weakly compressible, so
$\nabla\cdot\mathbf{u}$ is never zero. Over the snapshot grid, excluding the
cylinder and a two-cell halo, its r.m.s.\ is $2.46\%$ of $|\nabla\mathbf{u}|$,
against $\mathrm{Ma}^2 = 0.75\%$. A spectral decomposition separates two parts.
The time-mean part, the steady compressibility of the mean flow, is unchanged
from the earlier dataset. The fluctuating part is broadband and strongest in
the far wake; it is a property of the longer domain, not of the absorbing layer
(the same geometry without the layer carries the same level), and the
coherent duct mode that dominated it before is gone.

\begin{figure}[h]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{validation.png}
\caption{How the ground truth was validated. (a) Wake-vorticity $\St$: without
an absorbing layer the wake locks onto the transverse duct mode given enough
time; a viscous layer does not prevent it; relaxation toward the free stream
does. (b) $\Cd$ error at $D = 32$ with the layer: the inlet distance was a
larger geometric error than the domain height. (c) Grid convergence at the
original inlet distance.}
\label{fig:validation}
\end{figure}

\begin{figure}[h]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.92\textwidth]{re100_v5_vorticity.png}
\caption{The reference K\'arm\'an street at quarter-period intervals, the
start of the record. These four instants are the four start phases of
Section~\ref{sec:collapse}.}
\label{fig:vorticity}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Measuring $\St$.} An early estimate of $\St$ taken from an FFT
peak gave a fraction-of-a-percent agreement that was pure luck: over a record
of this length a single FFT bin is wider than the discrepancy being measured.
The $\St$ values reported here are measured from wake vorticity averaged over
many points, cross-checked against a single wake probe and the lift; on the
production dataset the three agree to $0.002\%$, where on the earlier one they
disagreed by about $1\%$ because the lift carried the duct mode.

\section{An unsteady Navier--Stokes operator}
\label{sec:operator}

\texttt{underPINN} ships only a steady incompressible residual, which cannot
represent shedding at all. This project supplies the unsteady operator
(\texttt{src/pinn/ns2d\_unsteady.py}), conforming to the framework's
\texttt{BasePDE} contract so it composes with the existing solvers, samplers
and networks. Non-dimensionalised on $D$ and $U$,
\begin{align}
u_x + v_y &= 0, \\
u_t + u u_x + v u_y + p_x - \tfrac{1}{\Rey}(u_{xx} + u_{yy}) &= 0, \\
v_t + u v_x + v v_y + p_y - \tfrac{1}{\Rey}(v_{xx} + v_{yy}) &= 0,
\end{align}
with the network mapping $(x,y,t) \mapsto (u,v,p)$.

Two derivative backends are implemented: a literal \texttt{jax.hessian}
reference, and a forward-over-forward JVP path computing only the six
derivative groups the residual needs, where a full Hessian would compute 27.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{Verification of the unsteady operator. All three checks pass at
machine precision.}
\begin{tabular}{lc}
\toprule
check & result \\
\midrule
annihilates the Taylor--Green vortex (an exact NS solution) & $1.6\times 10^{-16}$ \\
fast JVP backend versus literal Hessian & $2.8\times 10^{-17}$ \\
steady limit versus \texttt{underPINN}'s own \texttt{NavierStokesPDE} & $5.6\times 10^{-17}$ \\
speed-up of the fast backend & ${\approx}2.5\times$ (load dependent) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The third check compares the new operator, in its steady limit, with the
framework's own steady residual, so it tests the new code against independent
code that was already in use.

\section{Reproducing the collapse}
\label{sec:collapse}

A plain multilayer perceptron $[3, 128^{\times 6}, 3]$ is trained on physics,
boundary and initial conditions with \emph{no data}, over a single time window
of one shedding period, for $20\,000$ epochs. Its initial condition is the
reference field at the start of the window, the one piece of ground truth
that any forward solve needs.

\emph{Shedding retained} is this project's own metric: the ratio of
transverse-velocity r.m.s.\ at a fixed wake probe between the PINN and the LBM
reference over the run. Near 0\% means collapse to steady flow; 100\% means
the wake amplitude matches.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{The plain PINN, by the phase of the shedding cycle at which it is
started. Quarter-period steps, five seeds each, seed means.}
\begin{tabular}{lccccc}
\toprule
start phase & 0 & $\tfrac14$ & $\tfrac12$ & $\tfrac34$ & mean \\
\midrule
shedding retained & 43.2\% & 20.3\% & 42.1\% & 19.0\% & \textbf{31.1\%} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\label{tab:baseline_phase}
\end{table}

The plain PINN keeps between 19\% and 43\% of the reference amplitude,
with a field error of 0.17: it does not reproduce the wake, though
within one period it does not collapse fully onto the steady solution either.
Which of those it looks like depends on \emph{when it starts}. Retention
alternates every quarter period, so it repeats every half cycle, the half
period over which the transverse velocity at the probe changes sign. Released
at a peak of the wake signal the network carries more of it through the window
than released at a zero crossing.

An earlier version of this report quoted ``10.6\% of the wake'' from a single starting
instant; on that dataset the same configuration gives 9.1\%, 25.6\%, 13.1\% and
34.9\% at the four phases. A comparison between configurations at one starting
instant is a comparison at that phase only, so every retention figure below is
either averaged over the four phases or labelled with its phase.

\paragraph{Longer training.} Trained for $80\,000$ epochs instead of
$20\,000$ (the budget a four-window marched run spends in
Section~\ref{sec:ablation}), the same network keeps 48.6\% on average, at a
field error of 0.115. Training longer helps, by 17.5 points phase-averaged, but
the half-cycle swing survives it: 62.6\% and 61.2\% at phases 0 and
$\tfrac12$, 34.3\% and 36.5\% at the other two.

\section{Defeating the collapse}
\label{sec:ablation}

Three mechanisms are implemented as switches on one trainer, so that the
ablation is controlled: every configuration shares the sampler, the
optimiser, the schedule and the evaluation.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{The ablation matrix: what each configuration attacks.}
\begin{tabular}{lll}
\toprule
configuration & mechanism & obstacle attacked \\
\midrule
\texttt{baseline}   & --- & (control) \\
\texttt{fourier}    & random Fourier features & spectral bias \\
\texttt{decompose}  & Reynolds decomposition $u = u_0 + u'$ & conditioning, dynamic range \\
\texttt{march}      & causal time-marching & weak initial condition, causality \\
\texttt{all}        & all three & --- \\
\texttt{all+data}   & plus $4\,000$ supervised points per window & --- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

There are three implementation details. First, the Reynolds decomposition requires a
\emph{differentiable} mean field, because the momentum residual contains
$\nabla u_0$ and $\nabla^2 u_0$; bilinear interpolation of a grid gives
piecewise-constant first derivatives and identically zero second derivatives.
The mean is therefore fitted by a separate frozen network (relative
$L_2 = 2.2\times 10^{-3}$). Second, that mean is obtained by \emph{regression
on the measured mean}, not by a steady PINN solve, because the time mean of a
shedding flow does not satisfy the steady equations; it carries the
divergence of the Reynolds stresses.

Third, the marching chain. A marched run solves four windows of a quarter
period in sequence. The first takes the reference initial condition, like every
other configuration; each later window takes its initial condition from the
\emph{previous window's network} at the shared instant, so the whole run
touches ground truth exactly once. An earlier version of this project instead
gave every window a fresh reference snapshot, so a marched run used four
ground-truth slices spread across the period against one for the single-window
runs it was compared with. The effect of that is measured below.

\begin{tabular}{lcc}

configuration & shedding retained & relative $L_2$ \\
\midrule
\texttt{baseline}  & 41.1\% & 0.173 \\
\texttt{fourier}   & 36.9\% & 0.149 \\
\texttt{decompose} & 36.1\% & 0.086 \\
\texttt{march}     & 72.2\% & 0.156 \\
\texttt{all}       & 77.3\% & 0.052 \\
\texttt{all+data}  & 99.1\% & \textbf{0.006} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\label{tab:ablation}
\end{table}

\begin{table}[h]

\caption{The three configurations the conclusion rests on, at all four start
phases (five seeds each). \texttt{all} uses $\sigma = 8$.}
\begin{tabular}{lcccccc}
\toprule
configuration & 0 & $\tfrac14$ & $\tfrac12$ & $\tfrac34$ & mean & relative $L_2$ \\
\midrule
\texttt{baseline} & 43.2\% & 20.3\% & 42.1\% & 19.0\% & 31.1\% & 0.166 \\
\texttt{march}    & 70.6\% & 40.4\% & 73.8\% & 40.7\% & 56.4\% & 0.156 \\
\texttt{all}      & 74.9\% & 70.2\% & 76.6\% & 70.0\% & \textbf{72.9\%} & \textbf{0.031} \\

\begin{figure}[h]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{phase.png}
\caption{Shedding retained by start phase, every run plotted. Marching lifts
the wake at every phase but keeps the plain PINN's half-cycle swing; with
Fourier features and the Reynolds decomposition added, the result no longer
depends on when the run starts.}
\label{fig:phase}
\end{figure}

Neither spectral bias nor conditioning is the binding constraint on its own:
Fourier features and the decomposition each leave retention slightly below the
plain PINN's (37\% and 36\% against 41\% at phase 0), though the decomposition
halves the field error. Causal
time-marching roughly doubles the retained wake at every start phase, not
only on average, though with four times the training (see \emph{Equal compute}
below); but on its own it inherits the plain PINN's half-cycle
swing, between 40\% and 74\%. Only with all three mechanisms does the result
stop depending on when the run starts: 70--77\% at every phase, at a field
error of 0.031, a fifth of either of the others. Over the five seeds the phase
means carry 95\% intervals of $\pm 1.5$, $\pm 0.9$ and $\pm 4.6$ points for
\texttt{baseline}, \texttt{march} and \texttt{all}: \texttt{all} varies most
from seed to seed, but nowhere near enough to close either gap. No single
mechanism is sufficient; the three are complementary, which agrees with the
interaction effects Shah\,\cite{shah2026} reports.

\paragraph{What the extra ground truth was worth.} The same marched
configurations with a fresh reference snapshot at every window, as the earlier
version ran them, retain 93.0\% (\texttt{march}) and 94.5\% (\texttt{all})
at phase 0, against 72.2\% and 77.3\% chained. About twenty points of the
earlier headline were three extra slices of the answer.

\paragraph{Equal compute.} A marched run trains four windows of $20\,000$
epochs, four times what a single-window run gets, so part of its advantage
could be training alone. Each marched configuration was therefore paired with a
single-window run given $80\,000$ epochs, at every start phase and seed.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{Marching against single-window runs of equal training budget
($80\,000$ epochs), averaged over four start phases and five seeds. Gains are
paired by phase and seed.}
\small
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
comparison & retained & retained & gain (points) & paired range \\
\midrule
\texttt{march} vs \texttt{baseline}, $80\,000$ & 56.4\% & 48.6\% & $+7.7$ & $-2.2$ to $+15.8$ \\
\texttt{all} vs Fourier + decomposition, $80\,000$ & 72.9\% & 38.7\% & $+34.1$ & $+20.0$ to $+55.2$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\label{tab:budget}
\end{table}

Alone, marching wins 19 of the 20 pairings and loses one by 2.2 points,
and it wins by less than the first table suggests. Of its gain over the plain
PINN, training longer accounts for 17.5 points and causality for
7.7. With Fourier features and the decomposition in place the picture
changes. Those two mechanisms on one window keep 38.7\% at $80\,000$ epochs,
less than the plain PINN given the same budget, and they still swing with start
phase; adding the marching chain lifts them by 34.1 points, in all 20
pairings, and removes the swing. Causality is worth more than four times as
much in the combination as alone.
Over the five seeds the three paired gains carry 95\% intervals of
$\pm 0.7$ points (training longer), $\pm 1.9$ (causality alone) and $\pm 9.0$
(causality in the combination). The last is wide because its one-window
control varies more between seeds than any other configuration, at
$38.7 \pm 9.5\%$.

\subsection{Hyperparameters}

The Fourier bandwidth no longer changes how much wake survives, but it lowers
the field error by forty per cent once the other mechanisms are in place, and
does little without them. A heavier initial-condition weight buys nothing.

\section{Shedding accuracy}
\label{sec:accuracy}

Shedding retained is an amplitude ratio: it answers ``is there a wake'', which
is the right question for the collapse and the wrong one for prediction
accuracy. A network could hold the right amplitude at the wrong frequency, or
drift out of phase, and the ablation table would not notice. The best
data-free configuration (\texttt{all}, $\sigma = 8$) was therefore compared
against the reference probe signal directly, over one shedding period and,
marched over twenty chained windows, over five.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{Prediction accuracy of \texttt{all} ($\sigma = 8$) at $\Rey = 100$,
one ground-truth slice per run.}
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
quantity & 1 period (4 windows) & 5 periods (20 windows) \\
\midrule
shedding frequency $\St$ & --- & 0.1476 ($-10.4\%$) \\
reference $\St$ over the same span & --- & 0.1648 \\
zero crossings available & 2 & 9 \\
wake amplitude           & 73.5\% & 63.8\% \\
phase lag                & $0.1^\circ$ & --- \\
phase error by the end   & --- & ${\approx}\,0.5$ period \\
velocity-field error     & 0.034 & 0.156 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\label{tab:accuracy}
\end{table}

Over one period the network holds the phase of the reference to a tenth of a
degree, at 73.5\% of its amplitude and a field error of 0.034. No frequency is
quoted for that run: two zero crossings are not enough to measure one, and over
the same window the estimator reads even the reference at 0.139 against the
dataset's 0.1648.

Over five periods the network keeps shedding (nine zero crossings and a
recognisable K\'arm\'an street, Figure~\ref{fig:fields}) but at a frequency
10.4\% below the reference. The phase error that accumulates from that is
about half a cycle by the end of the run, which is what the probe trace shows:
the two signals start together and finish nearly in antiphase. Amplitude decays
to 63.8\% and the field error grows to 0.156. A cross-correlation lag is not
quoted for this run, because with the frequencies a tenth apart it is ambiguous
modulo one period.

An earlier version of this report found the opposite ($\St$ within $0.1\%$
over five periods and a negligible drift) and concluded that the marching
chain does not accumulate error. That run gave all twenty windows a fresh
reference snapshot, so the phase was re-anchored to the truth at every handoff.
A chain that carries its own state forward does not hold phase over five
periods. Data-free marching sustains a wake, but on this evidence it does not
forecast one.

\begin{figure}[h]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.85\textwidth]{fields_v5.png}
\caption{The data-free PINN (\texttt{all}, $\sigma = 8$) marched over five
shedding periods on one ground-truth slice, against the reference. Top: wake
vorticity at the end of the run. Bottom: transverse velocity at the wake probe;
grey lines are window boundaries. The network tracks the reference for about a
period, then sheds slower and weaker, and ends nearly half a cycle behind.}
\label{fig:fields}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Visible artefact.} The probe trace has small kinks at window
handoffs, where continuity between windows is enforced only through the
initial-condition loss. Roy and Castonguay\,\cite{roy2024} enforce it exactly
through a solution ansatz; applying that here is listed in
Section~\ref{sec:ongoing}.

\paragraph{Sparse re-anchoring.} The earlier run held the phase
with a fresh snapshot at every window: $20 \times 4\,000 = 80\,000$ reference
points. Table~\ref{tab:reanchor} asks how few will do. The five-period run is
repeated with $N$ supervised $(u, v)$ samples, drawn across the window's own
time span, given to every $K$-th window (windows $0, K, 2K, \ldots$) and to no
other. Initial conditions stay chained throughout, so after the first slice the
anchor points are the only ground truth a run sees. The phase is scored as the
cross-correlation lag within the last reference period, which is unambiguous
while the drift per period stays under half a cycle; for the data-free run it
reads 0.37 of a period, a little below the end-point estimate of
Table~\ref{tab:accuracy} because it averages over the final period.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{Sparse re-anchoring of the five-period run (\texttt{all}, $\sigma = 8$,
20 chained quarter-period windows). $N$ supervised points go to every $K$-th
window. Two seeds per row, each listed; the lag is in shedding periods, over
the last period, positive behind the reference.}
\label{tab:reanchor}
\begin{tabular}{rrrrcc}
\toprule
$N$ & $K$ & points per period & total points & $\St$ error (\%) & lag at the end \\
\midrule
---    & --- & 0 & 0 & $-10.4$, $-10.2$ & 0.369, 0.345 \\
100    & 8   & 60 & 300 & $-8.8$, $-9.7$ & 0.327, 0.328 \\
100    & 4   & 100 & 500 & $-7.6$, $-9.1$ & 0.220, 0.318 \\
100    & 2   & 200 & 1\,000 & $-4.6$, $-3.3$ & 0.120, 0.100 \\
125    & 2   & 250 & 1\,250 & $-1.7$, $-5.7$ & 0.070, 0.185 \\
150    & 2   & 300 & 1\,500 & $-1.5$, $-1.3$ & 0.053, 0.042 \\
75     & 1   & 300 & 1\,500 & $-1.5$, $-2.6$ & 0.037, 0.080 \\
300    & 4   & 300 & 1\,500 & $-3.3$, $-3.1$ & 0.088, 0.107 \\
175    & 2   & 350 & 1\,750 & $-0.2$, $-0.7$ & 0.002, 0.002 \\
100    & 1   & 400 & 2\,000 & $-0.3$, $-0.2$ & 0.001, 0.001 \\
500    & 4   & 500 & 2\,500 & $-0.3$, $+0.5$ & 0.002, 0.003 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Up to 300 points per period the anchors slow the drift but do not stop it:
200 per period still leaves the run 3--5\% slow and a tenth of a period behind.
At 350 per period and above, both seeds hold the phase to within 0.003 of a
period over all five periods and $\St$ to within 0.7\%, on as few as 1\,750
points (about 2\% of what the per-window snapshots used). The threshold
therefore lies between 300 and 350 points per period. Near it the schedule
matters a little: at 300 per period, one anchor per period is the worst of the
three schedules on both seeds, while one in every window and one every half
period overlap within the seed spread. Amplitude rises with the supervision
too, from 63--64\% data-free to 74--87\% where the phase locks.

\section{Other Reynolds numbers}

each dataset's \emph{measured} shedding period, so all configurations span
exactly one period whatever the frequency; otherwise the comparison would

\paragraph{The result generalises.} At every Reynolds number tested, the plain
network keeps 24--45\% of the wake and the three mechanisms together 63--79\%,
and they cut the field error from about 0.17 to 0.028--0.040. The ground truth
holds up across the range as well: every dataset's $\St$ is within $0.6\%$ of
Qu et al. So the result holds across the two-dimensional shedding range, and
is not tied to one dataset. $\Rey = 100$ reproduces the main ablation's
first start phase, whose two configurations it shares: 38.8 and 41.5\% for

\paragraph{One start phase per Reynolds number.} Each run starts at the
beginning of its dataset's record, at whatever phase of the cycle that falls.
Section~\ref{sec:collapse} showed that the plain network's retention swings by
a factor of two with start phase, so the \texttt{baseline} column's variation
(24--28\% at $\Rey = 120$ and 180, 40--45\% at $\Rey = 80$) should not
be given a physical reading. \texttt{all} is insensitive to start phase at
$\Rey = 100$ (between 70\% and 77\% at each phase), which is why one phase is
taken to represent it here; that insensitivity was not re-measured at the
other Reynolds numbers.

\section{Sequence architectures}
\label{sec:arch}

Every network so far is a pointwise MLP. PINNsFormer\,\cite{zhao2024pinnsformer}
was proposed specifically against PINN failure modes of this kind: it expands
each query point $(x, y, t)$ into a short pseudo-sequence in time, $(x, y, t),
(x, y, t + \delta t), \dots$, and mixes the elements with attention. If letting
the network see a point's own temporal neighbourhood were enough to stop the
collapse, it would be a cheaper fix than marching. Two sequence networks were
tested: PINNsFormer at its published size (embedding 32, hidden 512, one
encoder and one decoder layer, two heads, $k = 5$, $\delta t = 10^{-4}$, its
wavelet activation), and the same embedding and head with a GRU in place of
attention, so that attention against recurrence is a controlled comparison.
One change was made to PINNsFormer: the PDE loss is applied at the token for
$t$ only rather than at all $k$ pseudo-times. With the published
$\delta t = 10^{-4}$ in normalised time the other tokens sit within $10^{-4}$
of $t$, so their residuals are near-copies; dropping them makes each network an
ordinary function $(x, y, t) \to (u, v, p)$, which runs through the unsteady
operator, the marching and the scoring unchanged. The protocol is the one
behind the phase-averaged table of Section~\ref{sec:ablation}: $\Rey = 100$,
$20\,000$ epochs per window, one slice of ground truth, four start phases and
two seeds, single-window and marched over four windows. The MLP rows are its
seeds 0 and 1, the two the sequence networks were run with, so they differ
slightly from the five-seed means of Section~\ref{sec:ablation}.

\centering

seeds per cell except PINNsFormer, run once (phase 0, seed 0); the MLP and
PINNsFormer runs at that phase and seed are compared in the text. Wall-clock is
the median per run on one A100, training and scoring.}
\label{tab:arch}
\small
\begin{tabular}{llrcccccc}
\toprule
 & network & parameters & 0 & 1/4 & 1/2 & 3/4 & mean & wall-clock \\
\midrule
single & MLP         & 83\,459  & 41.1\% & 19.3\% & 42.5\% & 17.5\% & 30.1\% & 6.8 min \\
window & GRU         & 287\,497 & 33.1\% & 13.0\% & 27.8\% & 13.5\% & 21.8\% & 14.1 min \\
       & PINNsFormer & 454\,619 & 34.9\% & --- & --- & --- & --- & 256 min \\
\midrule
marched & MLP         & 83\,459  & 72.2\% & 42.1\% & 72.4\% & 40.1\% & 56.7\% & 25.9 min \\
        & GRU         & 287\,497 & 45.4\% & 19.1\% & 43.9\% & 25.7\% & 33.6\% & 53.1 min \\
        & PINNsFormer & 454\,619 & 77.5\% & --- & --- & --- & --- & 307 min \\

\paragraph{Neither architecture stops the collapse.} On one window
the GRU keeps 21.8\% of the wake against the MLP's 30.1\%, and is below the
MLP at every one of the eight phase--seed pairs (by 3.7 to 15.1 points). Its
field error is 0.315 against 0.171. PINNsFormer keeps 34.9\% where the MLP
keeps 40.4\% at the same phase and seed. A likely reason neither helps is the
pseudo-sequence: at $\delta t = 10^{-4}$ it spans a negligible fraction of
the window, so the network sees no more of the time axis than the MLP does.

\paragraph{Marching is still what restores the wake.} Paired by phase and seed,
marching adds 26.6 points to the MLP and 11.7 to the GRU, and the marched GRU
stays 23.2 points below the marched MLP, with the half-cycle swing of
Section~\ref{sec:collapse} intact (45\% and 44\% at phases 0 and 1/2, 19\% and
26\% at the other two). Marched PINNsFormer is the one result in the other
direction: 77.5\% against the marched MLP's 69.7\% at the same phase and seed,
about what all three mechanisms reach (Section~\ref{sec:ablation}). It cost
11.8 times the marched MLP's wall-clock, about five hours a run, so the other
three phases and the second seed were not run. One run at one phase, beside
the marched MLP's swing from 40\% to 72\% across phases, does not establish an
effect; whether attention adds to marching is left open.

\section{Physics in a neural operator}
\label{sec:fno}

The reference paper's FNO is purely data-driven. This section reproduces its
recipe and then asks whether physics improves it, and whether the answer
belongs to the FNO or to operator forecasting in general.

\paragraph{Reproduction.} \texttt{underPINN}'s \texttt{FNO2D}, trained after
Renn et al.: Reynolds-decompose first, map two consecutive frames to the next,
apply recursively for ten steps during training with the loss summed over every
step; width 80, 24 modes, Adam at $1\times 10^{-3}$, 200 epochs, batch 16. The
record is split in time, never interleaved: the first 70\% trains, and every
forecast starts from a snapshot in the last 30\%. Two datasets are used: the
production dataset of Section~\ref{sec:lbm}, and the earlier one it replaced,
whose fields carry the duct's acoustic mode on top of the wake
(Section~\ref{sec:acoustic}).

\paragraph{Contribution.} A physics residual is added to that loss. The network
predicts $(u,v)$ only, so any residual containing $\nabla p$ is unusable;
taking the curl of the momentum equations removes the pressure and leaves
vorticity transport,
\begin{equation}
\omega_t + u\,\omega_x + v\,\omega_y - \tfrac{1}{\Rey}\nabla^2 \omega = 0,
\qquad \omega = v_x - u_y ,
\end{equation}
evaluated by finite differences on the grid. Continuity is available
separately as the cheaper variant. Both residuals are normalised by the
residual the LBM data \emph{itself} leaves: the data is weakly compressible
and second-order accurate, so driving a prediction below that floor would be
fitting discretisation error, not physics.

\subsection{On the production dataset}

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{Rollout error on the production dataset (relative $L_2$ on $(u,v)$,
held-out initial conditions, two seeds, pairwise mean of adjacent steps). The
trained horizon is ten steps, 0.31 shedding periods.}
\label{tab:fno5}
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
forecast steps & 10 (trained) & 20 & 30 & 50 \\
\midrule
\texttt{data} (paper recipe)              & \textbf{0.0010} & \textbf{0.0010} & \textbf{0.0013} & \textbf{0.0152} \\
\texttt{physics} (continuity + vorticity) & 0.0012 & 0.0012 & 0.0017 & 0.0364 \\
\texttt{physics\_div} (continuity only)   & 0.0012 & 0.0012 & 0.0018 & 0.0387 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Result.} The data-driven reproduction forecasts to an error of
0.0010 at the trained horizon and 0.0152 after 50 steps, about one and a half
periods. Neither physics variant improves on it at any horizon: both are
16--18\% worse at ten and twenty steps, and 2.4 and 2.5 times as large by
fifty
(Figure~\ref{fig:operators}, left).

\paragraph{Why this forecast is easy.} The error is about ninety times smaller
than on the earlier dataset, and the reason limits what the result shows. The
production record is a clean limit cycle, so every test initial condition is a
state the training portion already passed through at the same phase: held out
in time, but close to in-distribution. When the data term alone fits that
well, a physics term the data does not itself satisfy exactly (the
divergence of Section~\ref{sec:acoustic}) can only pull the prediction away
from it. This explanation has not been tested.

\subsection{On the earlier dataset, and across backbones}

The earlier dataset is the harder test, because its acoustic content makes the
held-out states less like the training ones, and it is where the physics term
does change the forecast.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{Rollout error on the earlier dataset (relative $L_2$ on $(u,v)$,
held-out initial conditions, two seeds, pairwise mean of adjacent steps). The
trained horizon is ten steps.}
\label{tab:fno4}
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
forecast steps & 10 (trained) & 20 & 30 & 50 \\
in shedding periods & 0.31 & 0.61 & 0.92 & 1.53 \\
\midrule
\texttt{data} (paper recipe)        & 0.093 & 0.183 & \textbf{0.296} & \textbf{0.365} \\
\texttt{physics} (continuity + vorticity) & \textbf{0.074} & \textbf{0.132} & 0.307 & 0.772 \\
\texttt{physics\_div} (continuity only)   & 0.075 & 0.140 & 0.312 & 0.764 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[h]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fno.png}
\caption{FNO forecast error against horizon on the earlier dataset. Bold lines
are pairwise means over adjacent steps; faint lines are raw (see the parity
note). The curves cross at approximately one shedding period.}
\label{fig:fno}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Result.} Physics lowers forecast error by 21\% at the
trained horizon and 28\% at twice it, then \emph{crosses over} at
step 27--32 across seeds and variants, which is 0.8--1.0 shedding
periods. Continuity alone buys nearly all of the benefit, so the effect is not
specific to the vorticity term. This is useful, because continuity is much
cheaper to compute.

\paragraph{Late horizons.} By 50
steps both variants have failed: the error on the
fluctuation exceeds unity, meaning that predicting zero fluctuation would beat
either rollout. The data-driven curve flattens because it decays towards the
mean flow, while the physics-constrained
rollouts keep injecting fluctuation energy and overshoot. Across seeds the
physics variant reads 0.63 and 0.92 at 50 steps, so the gap is not
reproducible. On this dataset, then, physics extends the FNO's useful forecast
horizon, but neither model is usable beyond one shedding period.

\paragraph{Even--odd alternation.} Rollout error alternates between
even and odd steps by 24--44\% in \emph{every} variant,
physics or not: a period-2 mode of the two-frame autoregressive map. A single
step's error can read 30\% better or worse purely by
which parity it lands on, so all numbers in this section are pairwise means of
adjacent steps, and the figure keeps the raw curve visible. On the production
dataset the alternation is 4--6\%.

\paragraph{Other backbones.} The FNO is one of several backbones used
for this job. A U-Net\,\cite{ronneberger2015} (local convolutions in an
encoder--decoder with skip connections, which unlike the FNO assumes nothing
periodic) and a convolutional GRU in the PhyCRNet
pattern\,\cite{ren2022phycrnet} (a strided encoder, a ConvGRU cell whose
state is carried through the whole rollout, and a decoder) were trained on
this dataset under the identical data, loss, rollout and evaluation, data-only
and with continuity plus vorticity transport.

\begin{figure}[h]

\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{operators.png}

\paragraph{Physics helping short and hurting long is a property of the FNO.}
For the U-Net the physics term changes the error by at most 7\% at any of the
three horizons, inside the seed spread at fifty steps (0.148 and 0.171
data-driven, 0.133 and 0.163 with physics). For the ConvGRU it is harmful
throughout: 30\% worse at the trained horizon, on both seeds (0.043 and 0.041
data-driven, 0.055 and 0.055 with physics). Both convolutional networks also
forecast better than the FNO without any physics, with 31 and 131 times fewer
parameters; at fifty steps the U-Net's error is less than half the FNO's. These comparisons exist on
the earlier dataset only; the U-Net and ConvGRU were not rerun on the
production one.

\paragraph{Comparison with the reference paper.} At the trained horizon the
data-driven variant reaches $\epsilon = 0.093$ on the earlier dataset and
$0.0010$ on the production one, against the paper's $\epsilon < 0.1$.
Neither is an improvement on their work, because the data are not comparable:
ours is clean, periodic, two-dimensional LBM output at $\Rey = 100$, and theirs
is noisy experimental PIV at $\Rey = 240$--$3060$ with three-dimensional flow.
The comparison shows only that the reproduction works.

\section{Conclusions}

\begin{enumerate}
  \item The documented failure reproduces on validated ground truth, and how
        badly depends on when the run starts: a data-free PINN keeps between
        19\% and 43\% of the wake depending on the start phase, 31.1\% on
        average. Four times the training raises that to 48.6\% and leaves the
        dependence on phase in place.
  \item \textbf{The three mechanisms are complementary.} Causal time-marching
        on its own reaches 56.4\%, but beats an equal-budget single window by
        only 7.7 points. Fourier features and the Reynolds decomposition on
        their own do not help. All three together keep 72.9\% (five seeds,
        $\pm 4.6$ points) at every start phase, at a field error of 0.031, and
        there marching is worth 34.1 points at equal budget.
  \item \textbf{Two confounds inflate marching results}, and both affected this
        project's earlier report: giving each window a fresh reference
        snapshot (about twenty points here), and scoring every configuration at
        a single start phase.
  \item The best data-free configuration matches the phase of the reference to
        $0.1^\circ$ over one period, but over five it sheds 10.4\% slow and ends
        about half a cycle behind. Re-anchored with 350 supervised points per period it holds the phase
        over all five, at about 2\% of the data per-window snapshots use.
  \item Supervision is needed in small quantity: 100 points per window take
        retention to 87.4\% and 500 to 96.9\%, and further data buys accuracy.
  \item The ground truth needed two corrections, both of which would affect
        any lattice Boltzmann cylinder simulation with reflecting lateral
        walls: an absorbing layer
        that relaxes toward the free stream, because the domain is an acoustic
        duct whose transverse mode captures the wake, and an inlet far enough
        upstream, which mattered more for $\Cd$ than the domain height.
  \item The result holds across $\Rey = 60$--$180$: 63--79\% retained with all
        three mechanisms, 24--45\% without, against ground truth whose $\St$
        is within $0.6\%$ of Qu et al.\ at every Reynolds number.
  \item \textbf{Architecture is not a substitute for causality.} A GRU sequence
        PINN keeps 21.8\% on one window and 33.6\% marched, below the plain
        MLP at every phase either way. A single marched PINNsFormer run
        reached 77.5\%, at twelve times the cost, but one run is not enough to
        count as a result.
  \item \textbf{Whether physics helps an operator forecast depends on the data
        and the backbone.} On the validated data the FNO forecasts to
        $0.0010$ at its trained horizon and physics makes it 17\% worse. On
        the earlier dataset physics improves the FNO by 21\% there and crosses
        over within a period, leaves a U-Net within 7\%, and makes a ConvGRU
        30\% worse, and both convolutional networks beat the FNO without it.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Limitations and ongoing work}
\label{sec:ongoing}

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{No data-free configuration forecasts}
        (Section~\ref{sec:accuracy}). Whether the re-anchoring threshold of 350
        supervised points per period moves with the horizon, the Reynolds number
        or the network is untested, and each re-anchoring schedule was run with
        two seeds.
  \item \textbf{Soft window continuity.} The marching chain enforces continuity
        between windows only through the initial-condition loss, which is what
        produces the small handoff kinks in Figure~\ref{fig:fields}. Roy and
        Castonguay\,\cite{roy2024} enforce it exactly through a solution
        ansatz, on one-dimensional problems; applying it here would remove one
        source of the accumulated error.
  \item \textbf{Five seeds for the headline, two elsewhere.} The
        phase-averaged comparison and its equal-budget controls
        (Sections~\ref{sec:collapse} and~\ref{sec:ablation}) have five seeds
        per start phase, with 95\% intervals of $\pm 0.9$ to $\pm 1.5$ points
        on the plain and marched networks and $\pm 4.6$ on \texttt{all}. The
        phase-0 ablation, the supervision and Reynolds sweeps, the architecture
        study and the re-anchoring runs are two seeds each.
  \item \textbf{The equal-budget control has one budget.} Single-window runs
        were given the marched runs' $80\,000$ epochs. Whether either kind keeps
        improving beyond that, and whether marching still wins at a matched
        budget much larger than both, is untested.
  \item \textbf{The documented case is outside the sweep.} The sweep covers
        $\Rey = 60$--$180$, its upper limit set by the three-dimensional
        transition at $\Rey_c = 188.5 \pm 1.0$\,\cite{barkley1996}. The
        collapse this project responds to was documented at $\Rey =
        200$\,\cite{chuang2023}, above that transition, so what is reproduced
        here is the phenomenon rather than their specific case.
  \item \textbf{PINNsFormer was run once} (Section~\ref{sec:arch}). The full
        grid would take about 66 GPU-hours.
  \item \textbf{The backbone comparison is on the earlier dataset.} The U-Net
        and ConvGRU were trained only on the data that carries the duct mode,
        and on the production data the FNO's forecast is close to
        in-distribution. An operator test whose held-out states are new (a
        different Reynolds number, or a transient) would separate
        what each backbone has learned from what it has memorised.
  \item \textbf{$\Cd$ is a few per cent high.} Across the sweep it is
        $3.5$--$5.7\%$ above Qu et al.; keeping $D = 24$ accounts for about
        $1.4\%$ of it (Section~\ref{sec:acoustic}), and the rest has not been
        separated. Nothing in this report depends on $\Cd$: every PINN and
        operator result is scored against velocity fields and wake probes.
\end{itemize}
